## Project overview

This STAT 330 project examines which academic, behavioral, psychological, and
circadian characteristics are associated with poor sleep quality among
undergraduate students. Using the SleepStudy dataset, the analysis focuses on
predicting sleep disruption—not establishing that any one characteristic
causes it.

The response, poor sleep quality, is measured on a scale from 1 to 18, with
higher scores indicating greater disruption. The dataset includes 253 student
observations and measures such as anxiety status, depression, happiness,
classes missed, weekday sleep, bedtime, and chronotype.

> **Key findings:** Anxiety status and classes missed were the clearest
> individual predictors in the selected model. Students reporting normal
> anxiety were predicted to have sleep-disruption scores 1.32 points lower, on
> average, than students in the moderate-anxiety reference group. Each
> additional missed class was associated with a 0.10-point increase in the
> predicted score, holding the other model terms constant.

## Modeling approach

The team first explored multiple linear regression for cognitive performance,
but its explanatory power was low. The project then focused on poor sleep
quality, for which candidate models explained more variation. LASSO
regularization screened potential predictors; best-subset models were compared
using adjusted *R*², Mallows' *C*ₚ, Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), and
10-fold cross-validation.

The selected model balanced interpretability and predictive performance,
including main effects and interactions among sleep, mood, anxiety, and
chronotype measures. Its cross-validated root mean squared error (RMSE) was
approximately 2.39 points on the 1–18 response scale. The report describes the
model as explaining about 35% of the variation in sleep-disruption scores.

## Interpretation and limitations

The results suggest that psychological health and class attendance may be
useful markers when describing sleep quality in this student sample. The
selected model also retained some terms that were not individually
statistically significant; their inclusion supported the model's overall
predictive performance. The report's diagnostics found the linear-regression
assumptions reasonably satisfied.

These are associations from an observational dataset, so they should not be
interpreted as evidence that anxiety, attendance, or other measured
characteristics directly cause changes in sleep. The findings are also limited
to the students and measures represented in the dataset.
